query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled aging heat treatment applied to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will nucleate coherent nanoprecipitates selectively at the lamellar colony interfaces, reducing dislocation pile-ups and local stress concentrations, thereby enhancing room-temperature tensile ductility while retaining or increasing strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting semi-coherent phase boundaries prone to dislocation pile-ups and localized stress concentrations.
generation.intervention: Apply a single controlled aging heat treatment at a temperature high enough to promote nucleation of coherent nanoprecipitates at the lamellar colony interfaces but below the coarsening regime.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing conditions with prior heat treatment conducted under precisely controlled temperature and time to achieve nanometer-scale coherent precipitate formation without coarsening the microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent nanoprecipitates at the colony interfaces that modify the interface character and act as effective barriers to dislocation accumulation.
generation.mechanism: The coherent nanoprecipitates reduce the stored elastic energy at the interfaces by preventing excessive dislocation pile-ups. This decreases local stress concentrations that normally lead to microcrack initiation, thus promoting a more uniform distribution of plastic strain, enhanced work hardening in the ductile phase, and overall improved ductility while maintaining or slightly increasing alloy strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated state, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit improved tensile ductility (i.e., increased elongation before failure) and equal or slightly higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies, which suffers from limited room-temperature tensile ductility due to dislocation pile-ups at semi-coherent interfaces.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to be valid only if the aging treatment achieves nanoscale coherent precipitates (without significant precipitate coarsening or loss of the lamellar structure), and testing is performed at room temperature; deviations in temperature or excessive aging could negate the benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Precise aging parameters (temperature and duration) must be optimized, and the balance between precipitate size, coherency, and volume fraction is not fully quantified; thus, the extent of ductility improvement and strength retention requires experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical eutectic high-entropy alloy samples. Subject one group to the proposed controlled aging heat treatment (with varying temperatures just below the coarsening threshold and durations optimized for nanoprecipitate formation) and keep a control group untreated. Conduct detailed microstructural characterization (via TEM/HAADF-STEM) to confirm coherent precipitate formation at the lamellar interfaces. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation).
measurements: Nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and coherency at interfaces using electron microscopy
Dislocation density and arrangement near colony boundaries
Room-temperature yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation at failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging treatment fails to produce coherent nanoprecipitates at the colony interfaces or if the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility (with maintained or enhanced strength) compared to the untreated controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:The role of phase boundary in second phase strengthening
cited_evidence.text: It is a traditional method to strengthen alloys by introducing internal boundaries in order to impede the motion of dislocations. Unlike coherent twin boundaries with low excess energies, grain boundaries and phase boundaries are regarded as major strengthening agents for metallic materials because they are more effective in resisting dislocation penetration. In this study, the phase boundaries were produced through the eutectic reaction during the preparation of dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA. Thereby plenty of phase boundaries contained in this HEA were semi-coherent due to the low energy features. Given that interfacial strength increases with the decrease of coherency, phase boundaries of semi-coherence prepared in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were observed to be strong enough to accommodate high stress due to their chemically disordered features, as proved by the HAADF-STEM observation (Fig. 3b) and in-situ straining experiments. Such strong phase boundaries were essential to achieving compatibility of interphase deformations through enhancing the strength of FCC phases by work hardening effects so as to commence dislocation glide in BCC phases.

Dislocation substructures, such as dense dislocation walls (Fig. 3d) and dislocation networks (Fig. S5), were developed at the final stage of uniform plastic deformation and dragged on crack propagation. Although BCC phases were strengthening components in the eutectic dual-phase HEA due to their intrinsically large lattice resistance, which made them hard to deform plastically, the existence of semi-coherent phase boundaries played an essential part in balancing strength-ductility. Considering the brittleness of ordered BCC phases, the unexpected strong phase boundaries can prevent massive dislocations from penetrating, thus not only reducing dislocation pile-ups in BCC phases, which may facilitate the nucleation of cracks, but also promoting work hardening process in FCC phases by achieving dense dislocation storage.
